## Prerequisites

This tutorial assumes familiarity with the basics of [mlr3pipelines](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com).
Consult the [mlr3book](https://mlr3book.mlr-org.com/pipelines.html) if some aspects are not  fully understandable.
It deals with the problem of missing data.

The random forest implementation in the package [ranger](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ranger) unfortunately does not support missing values.
Therefore, it is required to impute missing features before passing the data to the learner.

We show how to use [mlr3pipelines](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com) to augment the [`ranger learner`](https://mlr3learners.mlr-org.com/reference/mlr_learners_classif.ranger.html) with automatic imputation.

We load the [mlr3verse](https://mlr3verse.mlr-org.com) package which pulls in the most important packages for this example.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(mlr3verse)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Loading required package: mlr3
```


:::
:::


We initialize the random number generator with a fixed seed for reproducibility, and decrease the verbosity of the logger to keep the output clearly represented.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(7832)
lgr::get_logger("mlr3")$set_threshold("warn")
```
:::


## Construct the Base Objects

First, we take an example task with missing values ([`diabetes`](https://mlr3.mlr-org.com/reference/mlr_tasks_diabetes.html)) and create the [`ranger learner`](https://mlr3learners.mlr-org.com/reference/mlr_learners_classif.ranger.html):


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(mlr3learners)

task = tsk("diabetes")
print(task)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

── <TaskClassif> (128x9): Synthetic Diabetes ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Target: diabetes
• Properties: twoclass
• Features (8):
  • dbl (6): glucose, insulin, mass, pedigree, pressure, triceps
  • int (2): age, pregnant
• Target classes: pos (positive class, 35%), neg (65%)
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
learner = lrn("classif.ranger")
print(learner)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

── <LearnerClassifRanger> (classif.ranger): Random Forest ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Model: -
• Parameters: num.threads=1
• Packages: mlr3, mlr3learners, and ranger
• Predict Types: [response] and prob
• Feature Types: logical, integer, numeric, character, factor, and ordered
• Encapsulation: none (fallback: -)
• Properties: hotstart_backward, importance, missings, multiclass, oob_error, selected_features, twoclass, and weights
• Other settings: use_weights = 'use', predict_raw = 'FALSE'
```


:::
:::


We can now inspect the task for missing values.
`task$missings()` returns the count of missing values for each variable.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
task$missings()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}


## Operators overview

An overview over implemented [`PipeOp`](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com/reference/PipeOp.html)s for imputation can be obtained like so:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
mlr_pipeops$keys("^impute")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "imputeconstant" "imputehist"     "imputelearner"  "imputemean"     "imputemedian"   "imputemode"    
[7] "imputeoor"      "imputesample"  
```


:::
:::


## Construct Operators

[mlr3pipelines](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com) contains several imputation methods.
We focus on rather simple ones, and show how to impute missing values for `factor` features and
`numeric` features respectively.

Since our task only has numeric features, we do not need to deal with imputing factor levels,
and can instead concentrate on imputing numeric values:

We do this in a two-step process:
* We create new indicator columns, that tells us whether the value of a feature is "missing" or "present".
  We achieve this using the  [`missind`](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com/reference/mlr_pipeops_missind.html) [`PipeOp`](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com/reference/PipeOp.html).

* Afterwards, we impute every missing value by sampling from the histogram of the respective column.
  We achieve this using the  [`imputehist`](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com/reference/mlr_pipeops_imputehist.html) [`PipeOp`](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com/reference/PipeOp.html).

We also have to make sure to apply the pipe operators in the correct order!


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
imp_missind = po("missind")
imp_num = po("imputehist", affect_columns = selector_type("numeric"))
```
:::


In order to better understand we can look at the results of every [`PipeOp`](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com/reference/PipeOp.html) separately.

We can manually trigger the [`PipeOp`](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com/reference/PipeOp.html) to test the operator on our task:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
task_ext = imp_missind$train(list(task))[[1]]
task_ext$data()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}


## Putting everything together

Now we have to put all [`PipeOp`](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com/reference/PipeOp.html)s  together in order to form a graph that handles imputation automatically.

We do this by creating a [`Graph`](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com/reference/Graph.html) that copies the data twice, processes each copy using the respective imputation method and afterwards unions the features.
For this we need the following two [`PipeOp`](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com/reference/PipeOp.html)s :
* [`copy`](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com/reference/mlr_pipeops_copy.html): Creates copies of the data.
* [`featureunion`](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com/reference/mlr_pipeops_featureunion.html) Merges the two tasks together.



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
graph = po("copy", 2) %>>%
  gunion(list(imp_missind, imp_num)) %>>%
  po("featureunion")
```
:::


as a last step we append the learner we planned on using:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
graph = graph %>>% po(learner)
```
:::


We can now visualize the resulting graph:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
graph$plot()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/index-015-1.png){fig-align='center' width=576}
:::
:::


## Resampling

Correct imputation is especially important when applying imputation to held-out data during the `predict` step.
If applied incorrectly, imputation could leak info from the test set, which potentially skews our performance estimates.
[mlr3pipelines](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com) takes this complexity away from the user and handles correct imputation internally.

By wrapping this graph into a  [`GraphLearner`](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com/reference/mlr_learners_graph.html), we can now train resample the full graph, here with a 3-fold cross validation:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
graph_learner = as_learner(graph)
rr = resample(task, graph_learner, rsmp("cv", folds = 3))
rr$aggregate()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
classif.ce 
 0.3589886 
```


:::
:::


## Missing values during prediction

In some cases, we have missing values only in the data we want to predict on.
In order to showcase this, we create a copy of the task with several more missing columns.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
dt = task$data()
dt[1:10, "age"] = NA
dt[30:70, "pedigree"] = NA
task_2 = as_task_classif(dt, id = "diabetes2", target = "diabetes")
```
:::


And now we learn on `task`, while trying to predict on `task_2`.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
graph_learner$train(task)
graph_learner$predict(task_2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

── <PredictionClassif> for 128 observations: ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 row_ids truth response
       1   pos      neg
       2   pos      pos
       3   neg      neg
     ---   ---      ---
     126   neg      neg
     127   neg      neg
     128   neg      neg
```


:::
:::


## Missing factor features

For `factor` features, the process works analogously.
Instead of using [`imputehist`](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com/reference/mlr_pipeops_imputehist.html), we can for example use [`imputeoor`](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com/reference/mlr_pipeops_imputeoor.html).
This will simply replace every `NA` in each factor variable with a new value `missing`.

A full graph might the look like this:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
imp_missind = po("missind", affect_columns = NULL, which = "all")
imp_fct = po("imputeoor", affect_columns = selector_type("factor"))
graph = po("copy", 2) %>>%
  gunion(list(imp_missind, imp_num %>>% imp_fct)) %>>%
  po("featureunion")
```
:::


Note that we specify the parameter `affect_columns = NULL` when initializing [`missind`](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com/reference/mlr_pipeops_missind.html), because we also want indicator columns for our `factor` features.
By default, `affect_columns` would be set to `selector_invert(selector_type(c("factor", "ordered", "character")))`.
We also set the parameter `which` to `"all"` to add indicator columns for all features, regardless whether values were missing during training or not.

In order to test out our new graph, we again create a situation where our task has missing factor levels.
As the ([`diabetes`](https://mlr3.mlr-org.com/reference/mlr_tasks_diabetes.html)) task does not have any factor levels, we use the
famous ([`boston_housing`](https://mlr3pipelines.mlr-org.com/reference/mlr_tasks_boston_housing.html)) task.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# task_bh_1 is the training data without missings
task_bh_1 = tsk("boston_housing")

# task_bh_2 is the prediction data with missings
dt = task_bh_1$data()
dt[1:10, chas := NA][20:30, rm := NA]
task_bh_2 = as_task_regr(dt, id = "bh", target = "cmedv")
```
:::


Now we train on `task_bh_1` and predict on `task_bh_2`:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
graph_learner = as_learner(graph %>>% po(lrn("regr.ranger")))
graph_learner$train(task_bh_1)
graph_learner$predict(task_bh_2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

── <PredictionRegr> for 506 observations: ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 row_ids truth response
       1  24.0 25.28194
       2  21.6 22.08385
       3  34.7 32.55664
     ---   ---      ---
     504  23.9 24.48223
     505  22.0 22.85879
     506  19.0 20.57652
```


:::
:::


Success! We learned how to deal with missing values in less than 10 minutes.
